Free Speech. The right to express ideas without government censorship or punishment, enshrined in the U.S. Constitution's First Amendment and regarded as foundational to democratic society. Though the Framers embraced the principle, American law has repeatedly strained against it, from the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798 to prosecutions during wartime.

Free speech is protected by the First Amendment as part of the Bill of Rights, adopted in 1791 as a check on federal power. But this protection has been contested from the start. The Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798 criminalized seditious speech, demonstrating early tension between free speech and governmental security concerns. A century later, the landmark case Schenck v. United States in 1919 established the clear and present danger test, permitting suppression of speech that poses immediate risk. Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. became the jurisprudential champion of free-speech protections, writing eloquent opinions defending robust public debate.

The courts distinguish between categories of speech, with political speech receiving the strongest protection, while commercial speech and obscenity receive less. Free speech is not absolute. Exceptions include direct incitement to violence, true threats, defamation, and national security concerns, though courts have gradually narrowed these exceptions over time. The Pentagon Papers case in 1971 reaffirmed strong protection for press freedom even when publishing classified government documents about past government wrongdoing and deceptions. Yet free speech remains contested. Societies continue debating where boundaries lie between protecting expression and preventing harm, particularly regarding social media, corporate speech, and speech targeting vulnerable groups.
